abdul_detroit_forum.title: Detroit Economic Club Joint Q&A (Abdul El-Sayed & Mike Rogers)

Steve Gregorian (00:01):

Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Good afternoon. My name is Steve Gregorian. I'm the president and CEO of the Detroit Economic Club. Welcome to today's very special meeting, 93 years of incredible speakers and networking, and that tradition continues today. I do want to especially welcome our DEC members. And if you're not a DEC member yet, give me two seconds to convince you. Your next prospect, client, job, maybe best friend, is right in this room. If you want to build your network and learn from thought leaders on our stage, we invite you to invest in yourself and join today. As we get started, I would ask you just to please take a moment and silence your cell phone so we don't disturb today's program, and we've got a tradition of always starting with a pledge of allegiance, so please stand and join me as we honor our country. The flag is to my right.

(00:56)I pledge allegiance to the flag of the United States of America, to the Republic for which it stands, one nation, under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all. You may be seated. Normally, if you've been with us, you know we have an invocation, but I checked with our clergy and they said you are all perfect and need no blessings today, so congratulations. All right, a couple of thank yous. I want to say thank you to WJR, who's doing their focus show live. You'll see them during lunch. Thank you to WDIV Local 4, Lawrence Technological University, and Detroit PBS for live streaming today's meeting. And a special thank you to my fellow members of the Michigan Debate Commission who are here with us today. This program is a result of those efforts and we will continue to do more.

(01:49)I do want to take a minute to recognize our sponsors and partners. Make no mistake, they are the reason that we can bring you programs like today. So thank you if you're part of the corporate sponsors. If you'd like to become one, see me at lunch. Happy to talk to you about the benefits. And the other thing I was going to mention is our fall season continues to be red hot. Next up in November, we will host Delta Airlines CEO, Ed Bastian, right here at the Masonic, and we want to welcome Ed with a really large crowd because Delta is so important to our region. So please get your tickets. Plenty more to come, get your tickets before they sell out. All right, we always say hello to our students. They're here today courtesy of our generous corporate sponsors. They just finished a private reception with both of our candidates, which is really cool. I would ask you to hold your applause while I tell you what schools are here today.

(02:43)We've got Catholic Central High School, thanks to MBC Loans, Frontier International Academy, thanks to Detroit Zoological Society, Loyola High School, thanks to Accenture, University of Michigan Dearborn, thanks to Albert Kahn Associates, and the best looking group of all, the AGBU Alex & Marie Manoogian School, the Armenian students are with us today as well. So how about a round of applause to thank the students and their sponsors.

(03:16)All right, some DEC election history I think it's really important I want to share. Today is the DEC 16th Senate election focused programs. In fact, we've hosted Michigan's US senatorial candidates in 10 of the last 11 elections. And this is what the DEC does. We bring you voices of people who want to lead our state. And just a few weeks ago, you might remember, we had both gubernatorial candidates on our stage. For today, though, I do want to thank both candidates, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, for choosing the DEC, and here's why. You see many organizations fought for this opportunity to host the candidates and they recognize the importance of all of you to the future of our state. So I am going to ask you for a favor. Please help the DEC maintain high standards of decorum by offering the candidates a respectful audience. And by doing so, future candidates will choose the DEC once again.

(04:19)And the last thing I do want you to know, since we are the Detroit Economic Club, the topics you'll hear today will focus on matters important to the business community, Michigan's economy, and business issues and policies. Other issues, yes, they're important, but we will not include those today. All right, the most important person today is our timekeeper. On time every time, that's the DEC. Please welcome the best timekeeper and the best in the land, longtime DEC member, JR Hasano. Thank you JR. And now it's my pleasure to turn this over to our moderator. You know him because you're up at 4:30 AM doing your emails and watching him anchor WDIV Local 4 Morning Show, and he is the host of Flashpoint on Sunday mornings. Please welcome the DEC's and my good friend, Jason Colthorp.
Jason Colthorp (05:18):

Thank you, sir. Thank you and hi to everybody. Speaking of the governor's forum a couple weeks ago, just a few more people than that one, I will say. And I was informed a little while ago, a little bit more media, 28 media outlets, including from seven countries that are here today. So obviously this is a big one. I know we have at least one collegiate outlet, the Oakland Post is in the house. They made themselves. So thanks to all the media that's here today. I think this one's going to be unique today and I think we're in a good spot because we all know this race. We've seen how nasty it's been both on TV in the first debate. They have another debate tomorrow. And while I'm sure my colleagues at XYZ are excited about that, I think we get an opportunity today to put all of that aside and focus on some serious issues and talk to them one-on-one and get their answers straightforward about policy, hopefully without those attacks on one another.

(06:22)So you guys ready to get rolling here? There was an invocation that Steve didn't know about. I think somebody said a prayer for no blood drawn, and hopefully that comes through. They're not going to be out here at the same time, one, and then another one, so one at a time. And the first one that I'd like to introduce today, give me a nice warm welcome, your Republican nominee for US Senate here in Michigan, Mike Rogers. Mike, how you doing? Good to see you.
Mike Rogers (06:56):
Good to see you.
Jason Colthorp (06:57):
You can take this one right here.
Mike Rogers (06:57):
Right.
Jason Colthorp (07:03):

So the candidates are going to get the same eight questions. And as we go, each question, you'll get two and a half minutes for your answer. If you run to that two and a half minutes, you will hear this.
Mike Rogers (07:18):
It sounds like you missed.
Jason Colthorp (07:19):

Yeah. I didn't want to make a Michigan State football joke there, but I think we missed the kick on that one. I'm a Michigan Stater, it's okay. We can hammer our own. And then you get a two minute closing statement. There's a second chime, right? What's the second chime for?
JR Hasano (07:38):
So two minutes.
Jason Colthorp (07:40):
Two minutes. Two and a half minutes for the answer.
JR Hasano (07:43):
Two and a half minute answer. Two minutes in, I'll chime once.
Jason Colthorp (07:46):
Oh yeah, that's it.
JR Hasano (07:47):
And I'll chime twice.
Jason Colthorp (07:48):
I just did this a couple weeks ago. So you get one chime at two minutes, two chimes when your time is up at two and a half minutes.
Mike Rogers (07:55):
Can you play the Michigan fight song?
Jason Colthorp (07:59):

We can. We'll play it every time for every touchdown they score this weekend. What? They're going to score a ton. I always have to do this. One daughter went to Michigan, I went to Michigan State. I'm good on both sides. All right, let's get rolling. Mike, first topic, we're going to start with Michigan's economic competitiveness. Michigan needs to get more competitive and attract new businesses and help the businesses already here and help them flourish. What is the single most important federal policy you'll pursue to strengthen Michigan's economy and how can we measure that success?
Mike Rogers (08:32):

So two things, and one of the reasons my wife and I got into this race was for exactly that. Over the last quarter century we've lost 200,000 manufacturing jobs, our median wage is now $10,000 less than the median average. That never used to happen because we built things here. I draw a direct line to those loss in manufacturing jobs. Highest utility rates in the Midwest, highest auto insurance rates in the nation. The first time homeowner now is 40 years old in our state, 40 years old. We have huge challenges. Adding more cost, adding more expensive utility bills is not going to solve our answer. I think we got to go the other way. So the things that we can do is make sure we have American energy so that it puts pressure on prices. We think we can do that, number one.

(09:20)Two, we have to keep taxes low. There's folks that want to increase taxes generally, number one, increase taxes on healthcare, number two, which I think is a disaster for our economy and your healthcare. Then you have the problem that they want to undo taxes on overtime or no tax on overtime, no tax on tips, no tax on social security. Those are powerful tools to keep the economy humming. I think we'll go back and make sure we do those. Here's the most important thing we can do, which is the only reason my wife and I got in this race other than a good business climate and trying to turn this thing around. Two thirds of our fourth graders can't read in the fourth grade. Two thirds. You have a 70% chance of going to prison or being on welfare.

(10:06)Let that sink in for a second. Two thirds of our fourth graders can't read in the fourth grade. If we don't fix this literacy problem, we are all doomed. I'm telling you, doomed. We have a plan that goes in with phonics kind of interdiction to get kids reading at grade level. We've seen it work. It's a powerful thing. My wife and I have been part of a group here around Detroit called Beyond Basics that's getting kids back up to reading level, fundamentally changing their lives.
Jason Colthorp (10:36):

Let me talk about tariffs here. They're hitting Michigan harder than any other state and especially the auto industry, which is going through a major transformation as global competitors now challenge US automakers and EVs and batteries, software, advanced manufacturing. And you just talked about this a little bit, but when, if ever, should the United States impose tariffs, and why are you better suited than your opponent to protect Michigan manufacturers from those tariffs and ensure that US automakers remain competitive?
Mike Rogers (11:07):

Yeah. So I've come out and said we got to end this Canadian tariff war. I don't think it's helpful to us. It's certainly not helpful to our automotive industry. But there are tariffs that have helped. The very fact that cars are coming back to the United States, including Michigan, from Mexico and China are because of the tariffs that were applied to help us, I think, correct about 40 years of bad trade policy. So you see that the Silverados come into the Orient plant, that's huge. It'll be a multi-billion dollar investment. General Motors is actually bringing about 500,000 new cars to be built in the United States, and we'll have some of that up here in Michigan. Those tariffs are good. If it's good for Michigan, I'm going to be for it. If it's bad for Michigan, I'm going to be against it.

(11:53)Excuse me, the Cherokee goes across that bridge something like 16 times between us and Canada before it goes onto an assembly lot, or a for sale lot or dealer lot. When they oppose these tariffs, I don't know if they didn't understand that or weren't concerned about it. If we don't fix that part, we're going to be in trouble. It just really is disruptive to the automotive guys. My thing is this, send somebody back that can actually go and get a meeting and fix it and advocate for the things that work and be against the things that don't so we can get them fixed. Sending somebody else back that all they want to do is gouge the president's eyes out is not going to help us. We don't have a lot of time to get our very low metrics up.
Jason Colthorp (12:37):

Quick follow up here, take 30 seconds. You mentioned how this was to offset the original trade deficit, but analysts at the time when the president said this said it's going to blow tariffs or it's going to increase inflation. We've now seen it rise to 3.7%. Does that mean Trump was wrong on his tariff plan?
Mike Rogers (12:56):

Well, I just think they over... When they went to Canada, I thought that was not the right direction and mainly because they didn't account for how integrated we are in the automotive business. And we sell, content providers here sell into Canada for cars that actually come back to be finalized in an American plant. I just don't think they factored all of that. So having that conversation to me is important, but think of this. I mean, Detroit Diesel's adding a third shift. They haven't done that in decades. We talked to small fabrication shops. They haven't added second shifts in decades. They're adding second shifts. That's good for us in the long run. We just got to get this thing right.
Jason Colthorp (13:36):

Let's talk workforce and skilled trades. Employers are struggling to find qualified workers and many Michigan residents and college grads are leaving for better opportunities, and state labor data is now showing that the workforce shrank by 158,000 people in just this past year. What can you do from the Senate to close the skills gap and connect more workers to good paying jobs here in Michigan?
Mike Rogers (14:00):

So we've been doing the tours around the state where these small fabricators, they used to have a question when you get interviewed and it was a measuring tape question. They had to take the measuring tape question off. I've talked to at least five. All of them took the measuring tape question off because they couldn't find a high school graduate that could do fractions. Think of that. My dad who's a shop teacher would be rolling over in his grave on this. We have a huge education problem we have to fix. I think that's why we should put shop back in every high school or at least be accessible to every high school so that you can get connected to the skilled trades. It's a job China can't steal and it's a job AI can't replace. And it's huge opportunity.

(14:42)And wages, if you look at wages for new college graduates versus wages for the skilled trades, man, skilled trades is winning that fight all day long. So we have to A, give kids an opportunity to be exposed to it in shop. I took shop, my math scores went up. I finally figured out, "Oh, that's what math is all about." It's an applied math skill and we just don't have it. Again, fix reading in the fourth grade, let's get math right. Why this is such a big problem, think of this, in eighth grade here in Detroit, only 15% can read at the eighth grade level and 12% can do math at the eighth grade level. This is a crisis like I have never seen. We all ought to be bothered by this. Any student that gets the eighth grade and can't read is shame on us. I think it's criminal. We have to change it.

(15:31)If we're going to help with how kids get connected, you got to do it in stages, give shop class, do apprenticeships. By the way, we talked to both unions and non-union shops about how they would use apprentice from high school to get them connected earlier in skill sets. I love this idea, we ought to do it. Get them reading, get them doing math. We can fix this. And this is the good news. It is fixable. We've seen it through this Beyond Basics technique. We put that in every school. People get back to phonics. We're going to have our kids reading again.
Jason Colthorp (16:01):
I also took shop, but I only got in trouble because I was always-
Mike Rogers (16:00):
... kids reading again.
Jason Colthorp (16:01):
I also took a shot, but I only got in trouble because I was always breaking the wood, acting like I was...
Mike Rogers (16:06):
Karate chop.
Jason Colthorp (16:06):
Karate Kid, yeah.
Mike Rogers (16:07):
I've seen that kid in [inaudible 00:16:09].
Jason Colthorp (16:08):

Yeah, that was me. I got in trouble. My dad didn't like it either. All right. Healthcare. We touched on this a little bit. Let's dive into this a little bit more. Healthcare costs are weighing heavily on both employers and employees. What's the most important change that you can make to reduce healthcare costs without compromising access to quality care?
Mike Rogers (16:26):

Yeah, I think transparency. One thing, a woman was telling me the other day, she went into the hospital, she had a whole series of tests, and on the way out, one of the physician assistants came in and said, "Hey, do you want another one of these tests?" It was a scan. And she said, "Okay, they're asking me. I must need it." They billed her for that. It was like $1,700. She had no idea. My argument is we need transparency. You need to know what they're charging when you show up. I think transparency is the number one thing we can do to start putting pressure on prices. And let me just say this about how we're not going to distort the system. Right now, Medicare pays about a flat rate, meaning maybe you break even, sometimes you don't break even. The way we subsidize Medicare in this country is private insurers will pay about 200% of the cost. You take all of that away, think of the costs we will have to add for these medical shops to stay open, for doctor's offices, for hospitals, for everything else. This is a huge problem if we do this because people haven't thought about the consequences.

(17:33)So let's do something different. Before we break the whole thing and ask you to stand in the back of the line, take Medicare away from seniors, which you're going to do, that they've paid for since they were 18 years old, we have got to find ways to put pressure on prices. You do it through prescription drugs, making sure Canada doesn't get a better deal than we do. You make sure that there's transparency in hospital billing, and you make sure insurance companies are open about their denial rates. You start doing those things, we're going to start putting pressure on prices.
Jason Colthorp (18:03):
Going back to the transparency example, another quick follow-up, if that woman needs that test and she can't afford it, what do we do then?
Mike Rogers (18:11):

Well, that's different if she absolutely needs it. But here's the problem. Why did they ask her to do the test that they later learned she really didn't need? That's a cost into the system because somebody's trying to make sure their numbers add up at the end of the month. Transparency, like any other business, puts pressure on those unnecessary medical requirements. We want them to get everything they need. We don't want no doctor at the insurance company who reviews it and says, "I'm not paying for that. We don't need any of that. We got to get rid of that." This is the way you get back at those high costs.
Jason Colthorp (18:45):

Artificial intelligence could boost productivity. It could disrupt jobs and entire industries at the same time. President Trump says it's larger than the industrial revolution and needs no real oversight. What should the federal government do to help American businesses lead in AI while preparing workers for the changes that it'll bring?
Mike Rogers (19:06):

Well, we definitely need guardrails on AI. I've seen it personally when I was chairman of the House Intelligence Committee. There was a test of a missile system that was told, and this was very early AI concepts, we want you to measure everything that hits the tip of that missile while you're flying, get there fast and get there accurate, but don't use the power in the back, we need those to ditch the missile if something goes wrong. And it was a test. There was no ordinance on it. And what happened was in flight, the thing decided all on its own, go around, get use of the batteries because if my primary mission is faster and more accurate, I need that extra power. It gave you a little bead of sweat on your forehead. This was back, I left Congress in 2014. You think about what happened and how fast this stuff has advanced. We must have guardrails. There is a national security framework, it's something I'll support when I get there. I need to go through the details of the bill, see if it can't be improved. But the other one, and this is for the business crowd here, the antitrust provisions prevent these AI companies from cooperating on safety. I think we ought to tailor a very narrowly crafted exemption so that you can cooperate on safety. One of these companies is going to see something that they know is not going to work, if the other company doesn't see it, they plow through it. My argument is let's have that narrowly crafted antitrust exemption so you can talk to each other on safety, not on anything else in the business, but on safety. Those are two reasons or two ways I think we can help put guardrails on AI.
Jason Colthorp (20:40):

Michigan's per capita income, it's fallen to 40th in the nation and it used to be 16th, just 25 years ago, at least in 1999, which raises concerns about the state's long-term economic prosperity. If Michigan was just average, people would have an extra $9,500 a year in per capita income. What sort of legislation can you target to help Michiganders raise their income?
Mike Rogers (21:02):

So we lost 200,000 manufacturing jobs since 2000, 200,000. Those are all middle class families. Those are all higher wage jobs. We just have to stop the bleeding. We used to build a lot of things in this state, submarine components, under 700-foot ships, airplanes, the main battle tank in Warren, that's all gone. Now still happens in the United States, just doesn't happen here anymore. So one of the things that I've already had conversations with people about, you know what the Navy needs now? Under 700-foot ships. Guess what we can do right here in Michigan up in the Bay City area? We can build under 700-foot ships. We have talent, we have people. Guess what? Those wages are really good. Welders now are making over a hundred grand a year. Welders, not too many years out of school, you're clocking in at 100,000 bucks. Those are real jobs.

(21:51)I'm going to get Michigan back in the defense industrial base work. We should be doing it. Think of all drones. Even for drones, you got to bend metal to make these things. Who better to do that than the great state of Michigan? We know that these contracts are coming. We ought to help Michiganders be a part of the arsenal of democracy again. That's how our wages got up. And it also spurs civilian use. Manufacturing always follows these guys everywhere they go. We want to be a part of that for our future. That's the one way we have to get jobs up. Advanced manufacturing is pretty spectacular.

(22:26)We ought to be the leaders right here in Michigan. I think we can, it just takes a US senator who cares about it, who shows up, who knows how to put the right people in the right room to get those things done so we can build ships and submarine components. We can build drone activity. I'd love to get back in the airplane business. We have a huge aerospace industry here. Most people don't know it. We even have a company here that builds for SpaceX. Nobody even knows they exist. It's not because they don't want to, they're just real quiet about it. And my argument is we have the technology, we have the people, we have the know-how, it just takes somebody to put the right people in the room to get it done. That's what I'm going to do. That'll get our wages up.
Jason Colthorp (23:03):
A quick follow-up, if you have to work with a Democratic Michigan governor, big if, nothing's decided, but you confident in how you could do that?
Mike Rogers (23:09):

I don't care who it is, honestly. If you care about building the state and retaining manufacturing, put me in, coach. I mean, think about it. We have a housing plan. We're going to make sure that young people have an opportunity to get into houses earlier. If you go on rogersforsenate.com, you can see that plan. It's very exciting. People in Detroit love it. It's going to be popular. We're going to do that. It has to be bipartisan. Getting kids reading in the fourth grade, it's going to have to be bipartisan. When I was in Congress, I'm the only guy in the race that actually had put bipartisan legislation together to get these things done. I don't care who's the president, I don't care who is the governor, we're going to get this done for the future of our state.
Jason Colthorp (23:50):

We'll dive more into housing in a hot second. Let me first ask you about taxes. How would you change the federal tax policy to encourage economic growth while also addressing the national debt, which is exploding? What trade-off would you be willing to make to achieve both of those goals?
Mike Rogers (24:06):

So we just saw a figure the other day, $500 billion in fraud payments. Now, I'm a tech guy, I've been in the cybersecurity business despite what you see on TV, I've been in the cybersecurity business for the last decade. There are great mechanisms to make sure you can reduce fraudulent payments by using a little bit of technology. It doesn't even have to be a lot. Problem is with the federal government, they're back 20 years, they still have fax machines. Think of that. And so what we've got to do is make sure that we get after that $500 billion of fraud. I would try to eke every dollar out of that.

(24:44)On taxes, we need to make sure we have a lower tax rate that businesses can invest and some certainty on it. This whole up and down and up and down is not good for a business owner. We need a little certainty so they know how to invest. I'm big in research and development opportunities and tax relief for companies that are investing in the future of those companies, and that means the future jobs in those companies for Michiganders. All of that we have to do and we need to make sure that we don't have the largest tax increase in the history of the country, which is...

(25:16)I mean, that's what the other team is talking about doing. That Green New Deal, if you like your utility bill and the folks who are talking about this Green New Deal, since we did a mini one in the state in 2023, this is a Democrat-led operation, they've raised our utility rates nine times because the mandates on our companies are not doable. So they're trying to figure out how they meet the law, and guess who's paying for that? We are all paying for that. If you want a company here, give them cheaper rates, make sure their insurance rates, their auto insurance rates aren't the highest in the country, their tax rates are low. We need to open up a sign and say Michigan is open for business again. Let's be the work belt of the Midwest again.
Jason Colthorp (26:02):
Just quickly, what about accountability on the jobs they promised? The Detroit News did a recent study saying they're only delivering on 9% of those.
Mike Rogers (26:10):

I'm always skeptical of an MEDC type investment, I'll be candid with you, because they never can quite promise what they can fulfill. What if we just took a step back and say we're going to have the best utility rates in the nation? Remember, we're competing with Ohio and Indiana. We're higher than Ohio and Indiana. Our state income tax rate is almost twice as much as it is in Ohio and Indiana. Wonder why Ohio and Indiana are getting these manufacturing companies. Remember in the last eight years we lost 27,000 manufacturing jobs, the rest of the country gained a hundred thousand jobs in manufacturing. That's what we've got to fix.
Jason Colthorp (26:50):

Let's finish with housing affordability and attracting talent here to the state. I mentioned inflation up to 3.7% now, which was the biggest jump last month since May, and rent is now one of the more concerning costs for people, and of course that factors in to finding workers who are willing to live here. Mortgage rates up to 7.25%, which you touched on, for a 30-year fixed mortgage, which makes the American dream out of touch for people under 40. What do you plan to do in the Senate to make those housing costs more affordable for Michiganders? And I know you touched on this, but maybe dive a little deeper.
Mike Rogers (27:22):

Yeah. I mean, I'd love to talk about our housing plan. Think about Detroit. We have 122,000 vacant lots in this city. We pride ourselves in how many houses we tear down in the city of Detroit. That's a metric they use every year. My argument is stop that, let's start talking about how many houses we build in the city of Detroit. How do we get them to do that? In my plan, you put all of those lots in a land bank, you allow builders to bid on those lots. Let's get it pre-approved for the city council. I've already been talking with city council members here in the city of Detroit about, "Hey, would you work with me on this if we could get it done?" " Yes." So that you have a much cleaner, less regulatory burden to build that house.

(28:06)And why you give them... When they build and they sell it to a family here in Detroit, it's 100% tax-free. Whatever you make on that, federally tax-free, I'd like the state to join in too. Why you do that is because builders tell you they won't build because they can't get the valuation to get their credit lines right. So that house doesn't kind of value it where they can get the loan for it. We're going to try to flip the math on that. I think this is really very exciting. So we've already got land that we think we can do it, and we're also going to expand it by eliminating in Detroit food deserts. I've already had conversations with some commercial enterprise folks who, if we get this right, we can have houses being built, we have students from the high school participating in the apprenticeship of building these homes and giving them a skill set.

(28:54)They don't have to travel outside of the city. So many Detroit seniors have to travel outside the city to go to the grocery store. We can do this. We just got a little creative. That's how we start this thing. Once you get one, you get two. And by the way, this works in Flint, it works in Saginaw, works in Grand Rapids. I mean, any city that wanted to participate, you can do this because you're incentivizing...

(29:15)And here's another thing. We have two of the largest financial lenders in the country. Guess who's going to help us participate in making sure these folks get their qualified for a loan? Well, guess what? I think we're going to get them both. One has expressed an interest. We're going to get this done. So it's a one shop deal, people moving in, we're building, we're going to have a new grocery store. I'm pretty excited about it. And here's the thing, I know Detroiters are well. We've had this conversation with a lot of them.
Jason Colthorp (29:42):
Take two minutes for a closing statement.
Mike Rogers (29:43):

Well, thank you. Listen, it just happens to... When I first ran, I talked about the issues that got us in, the jobs, the education, the fact that we're 46 in economic opportunity now in Michigan. We have to change all of that. I do believe something else is on the ballot here. This really isn't left or right anymore. We have built coalitions that really are very untraditional for a Republican candidate. We've spent a lot of time here in Detroit, Flint, Pontiac, I think if we're going to get our state right, we have to have everybody included in this forward progress. Can't do it without education. We can't do it without the right kind of framework to encourage building and other things, get our kids interested in the skilled trades, which I think we can. All of that I think is on the ballot.

(30:29)There are two very different visions. I had a elected Democrat tell me the other day, she was very helpful to me, and I said, "Why are you doing this?" And she said, "I'll tell you. We did it. We did it. Abdul, you did it.
(00:29)Good job. So proud of you.
Abdul El-Sayed (00:29):
[inaudible 00:00:30].
Good job.
Curtis Hertel (00:43):

I'm Curtis Hertel. I'm the chair of the Michigan Democratic Party. Well, it has been a long night, but it's also been a long two years for the people of Michigan. The people of Michigan were promised by this president that their wages would go up, that their prices would go down, that they'd be tired of winning, that there'd be no more foreign wars, the Epstein files would be released, and all of that has been a lot. And what I can tell you is the energy, the enthusiasm, and the fight is on the Democratic side. Yesterday was the highest turnout for Democrats in the history of a Michigan primary. And more importantly, over 500,000 more Michiganders voted in the Democratic primary than in the Republican primary. We have a great ticket. Oh, Jocelyn Benson, our current Secretary of State who has fought for our voting rights, will be our next governor. Eli Savit, who's been both a prosecutor, and a fighter against corporations that have poisoned our water will be our next Attorney General. Garlin Gilchrist, who has been an amazing Lieutenant Governor who has fought to end a Republican rule in Lansing, and has passed the largest tax cut for working families in history, bought 30,000 kids out of poverty, and ended the first state in 70 years to end right to work, past the largest investment in education, the largest investment in housing, will be our next Secretary of State. And after last night, a fighter, a true fighter, and that is what people want, Abdul El-Sayed will be our next U.S. Senator. It's been a long campaign across Michigan, and a huge turnout of excitement. But what's important is that Democrats are united.
That's right.
Curtis Hertel (03:31):

We are united in the fact that every person deserves healthcare in this country. We are united in the fact that the cost of living is too high for American families. That it is ridiculous that a family has to decide between the cost of prescription drugs and the cost of rent or housing, that they can decide whether they can afford to take that vacation, or even send their kids to college. It has become impossible to raise a family in Trump's America, and so we have got to work together to take this country back. And I can tell you, what we need as a fighter and a public servant.
That's right.
Curtis Hertel (04:26):

Whether it is in the Detroit Health Department, or the Wayne County Health Department, Abdul El-Sayed has been a fighter for the people over and over again. He has stood up to corporations, and made sure that the people are always at the front of the line when it comes to their needs. And we juxtapose that against Mike Rogers, Mike Rogers served in the U.S. Congress, left there, and enriched himself from the work that he had done. Made millions of dollars on the backs of people fighting for corporate greed over and over again. He moved to Florida, and then he decided to move back to Michigan when he decided he wanted to be a U.S. Senator. The people of Michigan said no two years ago, and they are going to say no again in 2026.

(05:21)And what I can tell you is that I'm proud as the chairman of this party, we have a very diverse ticket, but most importantly, what we have is a ticket of fighters. And we are proud to have Abdul El-Sayed added to this ticket. We are excited to say that he will be the next senator here in Michigan. And now I get to pass it on to another fighter. I've gotten to serve with Mallory McMorrow in the Senate. She has been one of the best fighters for Michigan. Someone who has always stood up. Someone who knows how important this election will be. Somebody who helped get us a trifecta to change Michigan for the better for people. My friend, State Senator, Mallory McMorrow.
Mallory McMorrow (06:27):
Good morning, Michigan.
Morning.
Mallory McMorrow (06:30):
Good morning. Did everybody get a little bit of sleep last night?
No.
Mallory McMorrow (06:34):

Doing okay? I'm State Senator Mallory McMorrow, and I am so proud to be here this morning. It is an exciting morning in Michigan. And I know that this was a long and brutal primary, take it from me, I lived through it personally. But what is most important now is that we recognize that for all of the differences we may have had in this primary, that those differences pale in comparison to the contrast that we face in November. Now, in pure Michigan fashion, I had made a commitment earlier that no matter what happened in this race, that I was going to endorse the nominee the minute the race was called, and that I would be at their party. Well, Michigan decided maybe we're not going to the parties last night. So this morning, with all of you, this is the party, this is the start of a celebration of all of us coming together.

(07:32)Now, I want to say to my supporters, to the supporters of Congresswoman Stevens, who fought hard, and to the Congresswoman herself, thank you. Thank you for putting your name on a ballot. Thank you to everybody who volunteered. Thank you to everybody who organized. Thank you to everybody who poured your heart and soul into these campaigns for almost the last two years. We need all of you, all of us, to stay in this fight every minute going forward, because I can promise you that today Mike Rogers and Donald Trump are looking at Michigan, and they are hoping that these family fights that we had, that disagreements within the Democratic Party are the fights that we're going to maintain through November. They will be hoping that we are either too hurt, because we, or our candidate lost, or too proud because our candidate won to not be willing to reach across and bring somebody in, or just to be too sad to move forward. Well, this morning, are we ready to show the rest of the country what Michigan is made of?
Yep.
Mallory McMorrow (08:46):
Are we ready to show the rest of the country what it looks like when Michigan fights and wins?
Yeah.
Mallory McMorrow (08:53):
Are we ready to do it alongside a fellow girl dad, girl parent?
Yeah.
Mallory McMorrow (09:00):

And I just want to give a huge amount of credit, I mean, look, this is an ugly business sometimes, and I just got to meet Sarah Abdul, thinking about our girls, and the future that it's going to mean for them in this state and in this country. That's why I'm here today. I know that we share a why. I know that we all care about making a better future for our kids, and that is why I could not be more proud to introduce you to now officially the Democratic nominee to become the next United States Senator from the great state of Michigan. Please join me in welcoming Abdul El-Sayed.
Abdul El-Sayed (09:56):
I just want to say how grateful I am to my colleague, Senator McMorrow, Chairman Hertel, to all of our incredible supporters here.
Abdul El-Sayed (10:00):

... Hertel to all of our incredible supporters here, what a race. In the words of Muhammad Ali, we shook up the world. And I want to say just first and foremost, how grateful I am for the opportunity to participate in democracy. Now my family immigrated to this country from a place where there is not democracy. You cannot just put your hand up and run. And the ability to do this, to have our voices heard, to select our leaders, it is a gift that sometimes we take for granted. So to have participated means so much. And to my fellow participants, I just want to say how grateful I am to you. Senator McMorrow, you ran an incredible race. You fought to end the corporate corruption, our politics.

(10:45)You took on the power of APAC. You were willing to speak truth to a level of power that sometimes is unbeatable. And I just want to say thank you and how grateful I am to have your support here today. I cannot wait to see what you do next. And I hope that for as long as I'm in this work, that we can be in this work together. Thank you. To my colleague and friend, Congresswoman Haley Stevens, we shared a great conversation this morning. And I know that it was a bitter end to this very long primary, but I also know that Haley brings the best of herself to her work. She is one of the most committed public servants that she'll ever meet. She loves democracy like I love democracy.

(11:29)And whatever differences that we might have had in the primary, they pale in comparison to what unifies us. A recognition that so long as we want to keep our democracy, that democracy better be working for people and that all of us have to come together to make sure that we never let Mike Rogers see the inside of the US Senate. So Congresswoman, thank you for your race. And I have to say a few more thank-yous before we talk about where we're going next. First, I got to thank my wife, Sarah. Yay. When we decided to jump into this race, I knew that it was going to be tough for me, but I also knew that it was going to be particularly tough on our family.

(12:12)And the fact that she held it down alongside her medical practice, alongside making sure that our daughters didn't experience this without thinking life was just normal, that takes just an extraordinary amount of effort and sacrifice. So I just want to say how grateful I am to you love, and I'm so, so honored and thankful that we get to continue this. 20 years on, it's been a hell of a ride. I owe her a 20th anniversary on our 21st anniversary because we definitely didn't get one of those this year. To my daughters, I know that they're not watching, but I wish this meant I get a little bit more time with you, but give me three more months.

(12:54)To everybody who put their shoulders into the work, anybody who made a contribution, who knocked on a door, who made a phone call, who put yourself into this democracy, who gave us your stake in democracy, this movement, this moment is for you. And I just can't say how grateful I am to have earned the votes that we got. We took on a machine. You're not supposed to be able to beat $70 million of outside spending. A record amount of money spent in a campaign against a Democrat in a primary in any campaign. You're not supposed to be able to beat that. And what we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money.

(13:36)What we showed is that if you're willing to build a movement brick by brick, if you're willing to go and travel your state and have the conversations in rooms big and small, starting in moments when people aren't even paying attention to an election, but are paying attention to the price of gas and the price of groceries and the price of housing and the price of healthcare, that you can build a conversation that builds into a movement that defeats Goliath. This is what you all show. And my hope is that our democracy will never be the same. So when big pharma and big tech, when DC and Blue Cross come and knocking saying, "You know what? This is our democracy and we're going to own it."

(14:14)From here on out, we can always point and say, "No, this is the people's democracy and we will always own it." This would not have been possible without the incredible efforts of so many allies and allied organizations. I got to give a special thank you to my first endorsers. Bernie Sanders, the OG who came in on day one, put his entire shoulder in the work. I just hope that I can help to carry some of that load in the fight for working people and Medicare for all that he's been carrying for all of this time. The UAW. UAW.

(14:56)As a son of immigrants, son of a father who came to this country to build cars, I got to say that this is still the best place in the world to make an automobile and that is because of the fighting UAW, but it's also the best place in the world to build a family because of the fighting UAW. And our work is about making sure that the folks who want to sell our democracy off the corporations and special interests don't get to take that away. And I stand in lockstep with our UAW sisters and brothers. To the AFT, the National Nurses United, the AFGE, the AAUP, thank you so much for your work to all of the advocacy organizations who made this possible on the ground. Folks like the PCCC and Move On.

(15:42)Folks like the Working Families Party, all of the constituency organizations who knocked on doors and made phone calls, thank you so much for putting your shoulder into the work. I also have to thank all of our endorsers, 300 strong, who came in, spent their time with us, came from just down the street or came from across the country to talk about what it looks like to build a movement of the people by the people and for the people. I want to say how grateful I am to you. We built this campaign brick by brick. Back in April, I remember talking to a room of five people in a discussion that most people will never clock, but it was an opportunity for us to share a honest conversation about pain and about purpose.

(16:32)And I've been able to have 500 more of those discussions over the past 15 months. I trained to be a doctor and the single most important moment that makes a clinical encounter is that moment that somebody shares their pain with you believing that you could do something about it. I don't practice medicine as has been well documented by all of you, but I hope that I get to practice that part of things. And I've been able to practice it, but it requires people being willing to share their pain with you so that you can do something about it. That is a moment, a piece of vulnerability people give you because they believe that you can actually fix it.

(17:12)It's an investment, sure, in a campaign, but it more is an investment in democracy. And as we traveled our state, we were in living rooms in Lansing, VFW Halls in Escanaba, basements in Grand Rapids, churches in Detroit. I got to meet so many of you, Michigan, so many. And you shared both what caused pain, but also what brought purpose. And we forged a movement out of that to get money out of politics, put money back in pockets and pass Medicare for all to guarantee healthcare in this country. And for our troubles, the corporations, the special interests, who would rather get to decide who our elected officials are than let us decide who our elected officials are.

(18:00)They spent an unprecedented amount of money to beat us. Attack ad after attack ad, after attack ad, after attack ad. Wall to wall ads. But it turns out that the commercials are the part of the television show most people don't want to watch. It turns out that you can spend as much money as you want on lies, but it doesn't make them true. It turns out that when you're able to reach out and dignify somebody's pain, people remember that a lot more than a 30-second ad played on a loop on television. And it turns out that when the people want something in this democracy of ours, the people can get that thing if we're willing to do the work of that.

(18:42)And that's exactly what Michiganders up and down the state showed. 12,000 volunteers knocking nearly 10,000 doors a day to defeat an unprecedented amount of outside money, $70 million. But right now, as bitter and as divisive and as cynical as the campaign against us might have been, I want us to realize that there is so much more that unites us now. Because the campaign that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and their GOP MAGA allies are launching is already more bitter. All you got to do is look at the ads you're already watching on TV started today. They think that you want to use my whole name against me. Mike, listen man, if you can't say the name, it's Abdulrahman, keep the name out your damn mouth.

(19:34)I'll be happy to give you lessons. But they understand that the only way that they think they can win is to drag us into the mud, to believe the worst about each other, to believe that what divides us is bigger than what unites us. They want us to think that the reason some of us ain't got is because of other people got. But it turns out that the reason so many of us ain't got is because of the system that has corrupted our politics to take it away from us...
Abdul El-Sayed (20:00):

... is because of the system that has corrupted our politics to take it away from us. And that is the thing that we are taking on now. That movement to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, pass Medicare for All, it is a big movement. So if you supported me or you did not support me, if you voted for Vice President Harris in 2024 or you voted for Donald Trump, if you believe, like me, that you ought to be able to afford your groceries, if you believe, like me, that you ought to be able to afford your home, if you believe, like me, that your tax dollars ought to be invested in you rather than sent somewhere else, if you believe, like me, that a government of the people by the people and for the people is our birthright in this country, if you believe, like me, that we have a responsibility to stand up and walk with our union so that everybody has collective bargaining rights in this country, if you believe, like me, that you ought to have the guarantee of good healthcare in this country without some corporation trying to tell you what you cannot have and should not fight for, I hope that you'll join this movement now.

(21:10)I want to speak specifically to an issue that has been focused on in this race. To my Jewish American sisters and brothers, one of the most indelible memories of this campaign will have been the opportunity to break bread with you at Seder, to worship with you at shul, to be embraced by you. And listening to sisters and brothers who said, "I want to join this movement because AIPAC doesn't speak for me, because I understand that self-determination for one people does not require the quenching of self-determination for another people." That unless all of us are free, none of us are free, I want to tell you the great gift that you've given me. And to all of my sisters and brothers of the Jewish faith or any faith at all or no faith at all, I want you to know that my commitment to your safety, my commitment to Jewish safety is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.

(22:15)Because if there is one question of a political philosophy that ought to animate us all is what would build? What we do if we treated all of our kids like they were all of our kids? How would we spend our money? Where would we put our investment? How would we embrace one another? What kind of schools would we build? What kind of healthcare would we offer? What kind of jobs would we protect? And I say this because there could not be a greater contrast between that philosophy and the cynicism of Mike Rogers. See, Mike's a guy who spent 14 years in Congress with one goal, to figure out how to cash out the day he left. And guess what he did? As soon as he left Congress, after having taken corporate check, after corporate check, after corporate check to empower the corporations to pick your pockets, he went and he cashed out. Not in Michigan. No, winters are too cold for him. He's got thin skin after all. He went to Florida.

(23:23)So Mike, if you want to be a Florida man, go be a Florida man. If you want to golf in Florida, go golf in Florida. But I promise you in November, we are going to send you back to Florida. Mike Rogers is the guy who wants to put a data center in your backyard so he can make himself feel a little bit more manly by making an AI video. Mike Rogers is the guy who has never shied away from a DTE check so he could turn his face in the direction of Florida. Mike Rogers is a guy who will do anything Blue Cross Blue Shield wants him to do, including raise your rates. Mike Rogers is a guy who introduced legislation to increase the flow of opioids. He did that while I was in high school. Mike Rogers is a guy whose politics and vision and perspective are old.

(24:12)Mike Rogers is a guy who has never shied away from a corporation he could do a favor for. Mike Rogers is a guy who, believe it or not, went back to Florida so he can lick every single boot Donald Trump owns to beg for his endorsement. I'm so sorry. If you want a senator who's going to lick some boots, fine, go vote for Mike Rogers. But if you want a senator who's going to stand up to Donald Trump, then you've got your option right here. And what's funny about Mike Rogers is that he's like the worst of all versions of the Republican Party. He's the worst of the neocon version. I mean, he was in the House during the entirety of the Iraq war. He left because he got tired of it. And then he swore up and down he could never support Donald Trump until of course he was licking Donald Trump's boots. So now he carries the burden of both of those things. Is he MAGA? Is he neocon? No, man. He's just a corporate sellout.

(25:15)So Mike, I'm going to say right here, I know you're going to say no because you're a coward. Five debates, all right? If you're willing to stand with me and have a conversation, you and I both know that you will wither in front of your own crimes, but I'm going to make sure Michiganders know about them because at the time we're done, you are not going to have safe quarter from people holding you accountable to what you've done for them here in Michigan. We will send you back to Florida where you belong. Five debates. I'm hoping for an answer today. It's going to be a lot of fun, my guy.

(25:54)But I want to finish here because it's not about Mike Rogers. It's not even about Donald Trump. It is about who we are as a country. I worked in that building right there. In fact, you could see the window of my former office. And there are moments I had to pinch myself because my story in America is about as unlikely as it gets. But for an accident of history that allows my dad to immigrate to Detroit, to go to Wayne State University. I was supposed to be a cab driver in Egypt like my cousins. I would spend a lot of my childhood summers in Egypt. I'd spend them there with a front row seat to what my life should have been. Except for I got to be born in America where I got vaccinated against diseases that killed an aunt and uncle I never got to meet. They died before their first birthday.

(26:51)I got to go to amazing public schools, an incredible public university. I got my medical education paid for by a public agency at the NIH. That's what America gave me. Now, the crazy thing is I grew up about 20 minutes from here. And in traveling 20 minutes, I traveled a 10-year life expectancy gap. I got to meet kids who never got the opportunities I got despite the fact that their families had been here far longer than me. I know what America gave me, but I also know what America continues to deny too many of her own children.

(27:25)And a lot of my work in that building right there was about trying to address exactly that. And I kept running up against one thing. The kind of politics that tell us that we cannot invest in those children because we should be sending their money to deny rights to other children abroad. A politics that tells us that the corporations should do what they can and the rest of us do what we must. A politics that tells us that our democracy is there for the taking if you have enough money to take it. And so when the opportunity to run for US Senate came up, I realized that this was a fight not just against Mike Rogers and Donald Trump. It was a fight for the kind of America that can give what I had to all of her children. That is the work in front of us.

(28:14)This country of ours, this America of ours is more than a flag, it's more than a set of colors. If you're a patriot, then you better fight for an America that is America for all of her kids. That's what this is about. Building a movement to take our democracy back to serve the people who absolutely deserve the best of what America has to offer them. That's the commitment all of us are making. So whether you voted for me or voted for my opponent or didn't vote at all, we're inviting you to that movement to get money out of politics so we can put money back in pockets and finally guarantee the promise of healthcare through Medicare for All. And I am so honored, so honored for all of the folks who've already invested, to all the folks who have, and I cannot wait to meet you and let's go win in November.
Speaker 1 (29:08):
[inaudible 00:29:09] questions. Hands up for a question please. And say your name and outlet when called on. Start here.
Joey with Associated Press. You mentioned that you spoke with Congresswoman Stevens earlier. Can you talk a little bit about what was said and if she indicated whether she would be endorsing you?
Abdul El-Sayed (29:26):
She will absolutely be endorsing us and she will be fighting alongside us to make sure that we defeat Mike Rogers and win the future in November.
Speaker 1 (29:35):
The questions, looking for locals. Oh, here.
Arlette Saenz (29:41):

Arlette Saenz with CNN. This was a very tight race. Perhaps quite [inaudible 00:29:46] votes are expected about 15,000 votes right now between you and Haley Stevens. Does the fact that this was such a tight race make it more difficult for the Democratic Party to unite and also reach out to those reach out to those swing voters who might be looking and seeing, well, Democrats bring out their feelings?
Abdul El-Sayed (30:01):
Well, I'd love to get other-
Arlette Saenz (30:00):
... Looking and seeing what Democrats will [inaudible 00:30:02].
Abdul El-Sayed (30:03):

Well, I'd love to get others' perspective on this, but let me give you mine. You heard about the historic turnout. Sometimes intra-family squabbles are the biggest ones, but we all know that when we walk out the house, we stand united. And sometimes we got to have it out about the conversation about who we are and who we want to be. And I think, I'll tell you that the things that unite us are so much bigger than the things that divide us. If anything, when you've got 500,000 more voters who came out to be a part of a process to pick a nominee, that means that their voices have been heard. And we're going to build a movement that reaches out to everybody. I know not everybody's going to agree with me on everything.

(30:45)That's not how this works, but I do know that they agree with me on the need to beat Mike Rogers, and the need to hold Donald Trump accountable, and the need to provide people healthcare, and the need to address the affordability crisis that is making it so that all of us struggle simply because we ought to pump gas or go to the grocery store. And the need to stop fighting stupid wars we should never be fighting. There's so much more we agree on. I'm looking forward to unifying together. The Congresswoman and I, the Senator and I, we've had some great conversations about where we go from here and we cannot wait to come together and win in November.
Speaker 2 (31:16):
Dr. El-Sayed, what do you see being your biggest challenge moving forward?
Moderator (31:26):
We're going to let the chairman answer the questions.
Curtis Hertel (31:27):

Thank you very much. I appreciate it. As our future senator said, 1.5 million people showed up to vote in Michigan on the Democratic side. That is the largest, not only just in history, but it's also the largest gap in history between the Republican Party and the Democratic Party. So certainly all the energy is on our side. But I also want to say this. We hold a special responsibility as Democrats in Michigan, as Michiganders in general. Michigan looks like America. We are the most diverse battleground state in the country. And so we know what that responsibility is. And I can tell you what unites us. We as Democrats believe that every person should have access to healthcare. We as Democrats believe that we need to lower costs for families.

(32:20)We as Democrats believe that it is time that we focus our attention not on foreign wars of choice, and that are raising gas prices for every person here and the price of groceries for every person here. We believe that it's time to focus on America first. They say it, we actually believe it. And finally, I will say to my fellow Democrats, if that is not enough, if everything that is happening in this country is not enough to unite, how about a Donald Trump super majority on the Supreme Court that goes on for not just my generation, but my kids' generation as well? We have a responsibility to come together and we will. We will unite to take this country back. I guarantee it. Thank you very much.
Moderator (33:22):
Will you take a few more questions? We can go here, guys.
Speaker 3 (33:22):

Welcome back to my Michigan Public Radio Network. The Islamophobia is going to ramp up in the general election. What is the best way to combat that? What is the plan to combat that over the next three months?
Abdul El-Sayed (33:30):

Well, so I really appreciate the question. You're right. That's the only play they got. They're going to point at me, they're going to point at my name. It's like, "Well, he's different." That's the best you got? You can't actually talk about what you want to do? My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can't afford your groceries. You know what it is? They're BS policies. So he can point to my name all he wants. But I'll also tell you this, I've been an Abdul in Michigan my whole life. This is like the best place in the world to be Abdul. You know why? Because Michiganders are, they're bighearted. They're open-minded. They're earnest and they're gritty. And Michiganders are sick and tired of BS politics coming in to divide us when there's so much more we can unite to actually guarantee if we're willing to come together around it. So if all Mike Rogers got is that his name is Abdul and my name is Mike, you're going to be surprised how many people are going to be like, "Yeah, but that's the Abdul who wants to bring down the price of my groceries and gas and stop us sending money abroad and make sure that I got healthcare. So yeah, I like that Abdul over your Mike from Florida."
Moderator (34:45):
That's right. Who else is there? CBS.
Ed O'Keefe (34:47):

Doctor, thank you. Ed O'Keefe with CBS. You talked about, you addressed Jewish voters in the state and the concerns they may have. You were asked about Islamophobia. You know that the Republicans and others will seize on one other thing, and that is things you've said in the past. One of them back in April, after the attack on the synagogue here in Michigan you gave a statement about what had happened. Among other things, this is what we seized on, you said, "Hurt people, hurt people." And is that part of your statement that has caused a lot of concern for Jewish voters? Republicans are going to seize on it. What did you mean you regret saying?
Abdul El-Sayed (35:22):

What I mean is that hurt people, hurt people. That maybe if we're serious about ending the hurt, we should stop hurting people. That's what I mean. I condemned the attack. It was a vile anti-Semitic attack. And I think it's important for us to be asking the big picture question about what's happening now. You've got a Republican Party that is morally bankrupt, that is actively hurting people.
